questions.question: Why does the analyzer store per-path count and totalMs instead of a running average in each worker?
options: Averages cannot be sent through postMessage
Sums and counts from different workers can be merged exactly; averages of averages are wrong when batch sizes differ
Integers use less memory than floating-point numbers
questions.explanation: Mergeable partial results (sums and counts) are the core of map-reduce. The average is computed once at the end from the merged totals.

questions.question: What does `if (pending.size >= threads * 2) await Promise.race(pending)` achieve while reading the file?
options: It applies backpressure so the reader pauses instead of queueing unlimited batches in memory
It guarantees results are merged in file order
It restarts workers that have crashed
questions.explanation: Awaiting inside the for await loop stops pulling lines until a batch finishes, keeping memory flat for very large files.

questions.question: Why does analyzeFile call pool.close() in a finally block?
options: Because worker.terminate() is required before postMessage can be used
Live worker threads keep the event loop alive, so the CLI would never exit, even after an error
questions.explanation: Active workers hold the process open. Terminating them in finally ensures clean shutdown on both success and failure.

questions.question: Benchmarking shows `--threads 1` is about as fast as using every core. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Worker threads cannot run JavaScript in parallel
readline automatically uses all cores already
Per-line work is cheap, so file reading and copying batches to workers dominate the cost
questions.explanation: Workers help with CPU-heavy work. When parsing is a fast regex, I/O and structured-clone overhead dominate, which is why you should always measure.
